statement: A frog sits at 0 on a number line. Each jump takes it exactly 3 units to the left or to the right. After exactly 7 jumps, which of these numbers could the frog be on?

choices.misconception: I thought the frog could jump right and left the same number of times and end back at 0, but 7 jumps cannot split into two equal groups.
I thought 2 more right jumps than left jumps was possible, but with 7 jumps the numbers of right and left jumps differ by an odd number.
I thought 4 more right jumps than left jumps was possible, giving 12, but with 7 jumps that difference must be odd.
I counted 6 jumps to the right as 18 and forgot about the seventh jump.

hints: Think about how many jumps go right and how many go left.
If r jumps go right and l go left, then r + l = 7 and the frog ends on 3 times (r - l). Ask whether r - l can be even when r + l is odd.
Since r + l = 7 is odd, r - l is odd too: 1, 3, 5 or 7, or minus one of these. So the frog ends on 3 times an odd number.

solutions.reliable: Say r jumps go right and l go left, so r + l = 7 and the frog ends on $3(r - l)$. Because r + l is odd, one of r and l is even and the other is odd, so r - l is odd. The possible positions are 3, 9, 15, 21 and their negatives. Of the choices only 9 works, for example with 5 jumps right and 2 jumps left: 15 - 6 = 9. The transferable idea: the sum and the difference of two whole numbers are always both even or both odd.
solutions.elegant: Each jump changes the frog's position by 3, an odd number, so every jump switches it between odd and even numbers. After an odd number of jumps from 0 it must be on an odd number, and 9 is the only odd choice.

whyOnTest: Parity questions reward noticing that an odd number of odd-sized steps always lands on an odd number, which beats listing every route.
